system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2149-02-19 17:20:00 to 2149-02-22 15:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of recurrent left lower extremity cellulitis, chronic venous stasis, lipodermatosclerosis, bioprosthetic aortic valve, pacemaker, and heart failure was admitted for worsening left leg pain, erythema, and swelling unresponsive to outpatient oral antibiotics. She presented with a low-grade fever and a history of recent watery diarrhea. In the ED, she received IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and imaging ruled out DVT but confirmed significant subcutaneous edema. During her hospital stay, she improved clinically with IV antibiotics, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient continuation of vancomycin. Her acute kidney injury, attributed to volume depletion while on torsemide, resolved with IV fluids, and the diuretic was held at discharge. She was discharged home with instructions to complete a 10-day IV antibiotic course, hold torsemide and potassium until follow-up, and monitor for recurrence of infection.
problems: Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Adverse effect of other systemic antibiotics, initial encounter
Varicose veins of unspecified lower extremity with inflammation

Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to ___ 
swelling, redness, and pain to both lower extremities. We were 
concerned for an infection to be the cause of your symptoms and 
started you on IV antibiotics for precautionary purposes. After 
further evaluation and a discussion with infectious disease and 
dermatology, we concluded that the cause of  your symptoms were 
unlikely to be caused by an infection but rather a build up of 
excess fluid and a dermatologic reaction due to that excess 
fluid. We changed the protocol for the wound care to both of 
your lower extremities and your symptoms of swelling, redness, 
and pain improved. 

You also had an infection of your intestines prior to admission 
known as C. diff colitis. You were given antibiotics for this 
infection and fluids through your IV for rehydration. Your 
symptoms including diarrhea improved.

Please continue your course of oral vancomycin and wound 
dressing changes daily as instructed. If your condition does not 
improve or your symptoms become worse, please contact your 
primary care physician or present to the emergency department.

Thank you for allowing us to be a part of your care,

Your ___ Team

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. My legs have been getting worse—more red, swollen, and painful, especially the left one. The redness has spread down to my foot and it’s weeping fluid. I’ve also been feeling really tired and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were recently on antibiotics for a skin infection, correct? And you’ve had diarrhea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I finished IV vancomycin last month, then started penicillin to prevent more infections, but that’s when the diarrhea started. My ID doctor said it was C. diff and put me on oral vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re concerned the leg changes might not be another infection, but related to your chronic venous issues. Still, we’ll start IV vancomycin tonight just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I thought the vancomycin was for the C. diff? Won’t more antibiotics make that worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re giving the IV version only briefly. It doesn’t affect the gut like oral antibiotics do. We want to cover any possible skin infection while we figure things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. My mouth feels so dry. I haven’t been eating or drinking much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re quite dehydrated. We’re giving you IV fluids now. Your kidney values are a bit off, likely from low intake and your diuretic. We’ve lowered your torsemide dose to 20 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop the potassium pill too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding the potassium for now. Your levels are okay, and we don’t want it to build up. You’ll restart it after seeing your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable—no sign of infection in your blood. We’ve consulted dermatology and infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it cellulitis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They don’t think so. The spreading redness and weeping are more consistent with severe stasis dermatitis—your chronic venous problem flaring up. It can look like infection but isn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so the IV antibiotics aren’t needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re stopping the IV vancomycin. Your oral vancomycin for C. diff will continue as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my legs? They still hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dermatology recommends a strong topical steroid—clobetasol ointment—applied twice daily. A home health nurse will help you with dressings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the weeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should reduce the inflammation and fluid leakage. Compression and leg elevation are also key. We’ll keep your pain meds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. The nausea is less, and I drank some soup. My legs feel a little less tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your urine output is improving too. We’ll keep the lower dose of torsemide to avoid dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart rhythm and valve—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your rhythm is stable. We continued your warfarin and metoprolol. INR was in range, so no changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. The nurse reported your leg redness is starting to fade, and the weeping has decreased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I didn’t notice, but it does feel drier. Is the steroid working that fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. Combined with better hydration and reduced swelling, it’s making a difference. Your diarrhea has also improved, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, only one loose stool yesterday. I’m on day six of the oral vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Finish the full two-week course. No testing needed after unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if things keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I need help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will visit daily to help with the leg dressings and monitor your progress. You’ll use your walker as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—what stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. Torsemide is now 20 mg daily, and you’ll keep applying the clobetasol. Continue oral vancomycin until done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still held. Don’t restart it until you see your PCP. They’ll check your levels first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if my legs start looking worse again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the redness spreads, you develop a fever, or the pain worsens, call your doctor or come back. But it’s likely manageable with the current plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much clearer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work with the dressings and fluids. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of recurrent lower extremity cellulitis, chronic venous insufficiency, bioprosthetic aortic valve, and pacemaker was admitted for worsening bilateral leg erythema, swelling, and pain, initially concerning for cellulitis. She had recently been diagnosed with C. difficile colitis and was on oral vancomycin. IV vancomycin was started in the ED but discontinued after evaluation by dermatology and infectious disease, who determined the leg changes were due to acute-on-chronic stasis dermatitis and lipodermatosclerosis rather than infection. She was treated with topical clobetasol, reduced-dose torsemide, IV fluids for dehydration, and continued oral vancomycin for C. diff. Her symptoms improved, and she was discharged home with home health nursing for wound care, instructions to complete her antibiotic course, and follow-up with her primary care physician.
